description: How WIDE a string-producing expression is DECLARED. Snowflake computes a width from the arguments wherever it can and falls back to the 128MB conversion width where it cannot. Case-changing is budgeted THREE characters for one going UP (UPPER of a VARCHAR(5) is VARCHAR(15)) and nothing going down, because lower-casing cannot lengthen. Concatenation ADDS the widths, CONCAT_WS pays for its separator once per GAP and INSERT for its base twice. Taking a PIECE of a string keeps the SOURCE's width and not the length asked for, so SUBSTR(v, 1, 10) over a VARCHAR(5) is still VARCHAR(5). Where nothing bounds the answer - REPEAT, LPAD, REPLACE, any conversion to text - the width is the 128MB maximum. A digest, a name and a generated identifier are FIXED widths whatever went in, and encoding counts BYTES with a character budgeted four of them. NULLIF keeps its FIRST argument's flavour, widened by the second only within that family. The rules COMPOSE through nesting, through an aggregate, through a conditional, and they survive a VIEW, a derived table and a CTE. Converted 1:1 from query/StringResultWidthTest (now retired); the Java read every width through the engine's Java DataType API, so each converted claim materialises its expression as a VIEW and reads that view's INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS row. That row stops a string at the 16777216 a column can declare, as DESCRIBE does, so every width past it - a sum or a tripling beyond the maximum, an unbounded result, a conversion to text - reads 16777216 there (live-measured). Each test creates one view per claim and asserts all of them as ONE ordered row set. TRY_TO_UUID, which live types with its own UUID data type, has a test of its own.

INSERT INTO sw SELECT 'ab', 'cdefg', 'hi', 1, 2.50, 3.5, '2020-01-01', '2020-01-01 10:00:00', TO_BINARY('AB'), TRUE, TO_BINARY('AABBCCDDEEFF0011')
